sentences.text: Shuvosaurus is an extinct genus of poposaurid rauisuchian reptiles represented by a single species. It was a beaked, bipedal animal that lived during the Late Triassic.
Although Shuvosaurus looks like a theropod dinosaur, it is more closely related to modern crocodilians and was reidentified as a rauisuchian pseudosuchian closely related to Poposaurus.
The only known species of Shuvosaurus is Shuvosaurus inexpectatus, described by Chatterjee in 1993.
The original description of Shuvosaurus included three skulls, a partial lower jaw, and a partial atlas vertebra.
Shuvosaurus fossils were found in a bonebed containing at least nine associated skeletons and a minimum of 14 individuals based on femur counts.
Shuvosaurus fossils were collected in 1984 and formally described in 1993 by Sankar Chatterjee after being discovered by his son Shuvo.
The name Shuvosaurus honors Sankar Chatterjee's son, Shuvo, combining his name with the Greek word for lizard.
Shuvosaurus was thoroughly re-examined and redescribed in late 2023 and early 2024, when Lehane redescribed the skull followed by a complete skeletal osteology by Nesbitt and Chatterjee.
Most postcranial bones originally assigned to Shuvosaurus were later reidentified as belonging to other animals.
Shuvosaurus is classified within the order Rauisuchia, belongs to the family Poposauridae, and is placed in the subfamily Shuvosaurinae.
The parent group of Shuvosaurus is the family Shuvosauridae.

Phylogenetic analyses consistently place Shuvosaurus as a close relative of Effigia and the South American Sillosuchus, and until 2026, Shuvosaurus and Effigia were consistently recovered as sister taxa within the family Shuvosauridae.
The relationships between North American shuvosaurids, including Shuvosaurus, remain unresolved in recent analyses.
In 2024, Nesbitt and Chatterjee restricted Shuvosaurus to the material from the Post Quarry bonebed.
Shuvosaurus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Texas, United States.

Sankar Chatterjee originally interpreted Shuvosaurus as a Triassic ornithomimosaur dinosaur based on its toothless jaws and large eye sockets, arguing that convergent evolution was unlikely and believing the skull features were distinctly ornithomimosaurian. The species name inexpectatus reflects the surprise of finding a toothless, ostrich-mimic-like skull in Late Triassic rocks.

Chatterjee's hypothesis that Shuvosaurus was a dinosaur was met with skepticism by researchers like Halszka Osmólska, and later researchers argued that Chatterjee had not definitively proven the skull belonged to a dinosaur.

In 1995, Long and Murry described the skull material as a new taxon named Chatterjeea elegans, while Oliver Rauhut argued that Shuvosaurus was a distinct theropod dinosaur that evolved traits similar to ornithomimosaurs.
In a 2003 analysis, Rauhut recovered Shuvosaurus as a coelophysoid theropod.

In 2006, Nesbitt and Norell named Effigia based on fossils combining a Shuvosaurus-like skull with Chatterjeea-like body parts, and the discovery of Effigia proved that Shuvosaurus is a pseudosuchian related to crocodilians and that Shuvosaurus and Chatterjeea are synonymous.

In 2007, Spencer Lucas and colleagues proposed merging Effigia into Shuvosaurus as the species S. okeeffeae, and James Lehane revised his classification of Shuvosaurus in 2023 after the discovery of Effigia.
